items.readable_text:
Content:
We can find the velocity [MATH: v(t)] of a moving particle moving up and down the [MATH: x]-axis by computing the derivative of its position function [MATH: x(t).] This same idea works in [MATH: 2] dimensions as well.

Content:
In two dimensions, we can represent a particle's position using a vector-valued function
[MATH: \mathbf{r} = \langle x(t), y(t)\rangle,]
which gives the particle's position relative to a fixed origin [MATH: O] at time [MATH: t.]

Content:
Here, [MATH: x(t)] tells us how the [MATH: x]-coordinate of the particle changes with time, and [MATH: y(t)] does the same for the [MATH: y]-coordinate. As time progresses, the particle moves along a path, and its position vector [MATH: \mathbf{r}(t)] changes with time.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/15fb899793084d902c8d4f698fad35ed]

Content:
The particle's velocity vector is then given by the derivative of its position vector,

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{v} = \frac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{r}}{\textrm{d}t}
= \left\langle \frac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t},\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t} \right\rangle.]

Content:
In other words, we differentiate the [MATH: x]-coordinate and the [MATH: y]-coordinate independently with respect to time. The resulting derivatives are the [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] components of the velocity vector.

sections.normalized_html: The position vector [MATH: \mathbf{r}] of a particle [MATH: P] relative to a fixed origin [MATH: O] at time [MATH: t > 0] is given by [MATH: \mathbf{r} = \langle 6t^2+2, 2t^3\rangle.] Calculate the speed of the particle at time [MATH: t=2.]

Calculate the speed of the particle at time [MATH: t=2.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we calculate the velocity vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}.] Differentiating the position vector, we get

[MATH: v|= (dr)/(dt); = ⟨(dx)/(dt), (dy)/(dt)⟩; = ⟨(d)/(dt)(6t^{2} + 2), (d)/(dt)(2t^{3})⟩; = ⟨12t, 6t^{2}⟩.]

To find the velocity when [MATH: t=2], we substitute into the above: [MATH: v(2)|= ⟨12(2), 6(2)^{2}⟩; = ⟨24, 24⟩.]

To find the speed at [MATH: t=2] we calculate the magnitude of [MATH: \mathbf{v}(2),] and we get

[MATH: |v(2)||= sqrt(24^{2} + 24^{2}); = sqrt(2(24^{2})); = 24sqrt(2).]

So, the speed when [MATH: t=2] is [MATH: 24\sqrt{2}\approx 33.94] to two decimal places.

A particle [MATH: P] moves in the [MATH: x]-[MATH: y] plane (relative to a fixed origin [MATH: O]) with position vector
[MATH: \mathbf{r} = \langle t^2-2t, t^3-3t \rangle, \quad t\in[0,\infty).]

Calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we calculate the velocity vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}.] Differentiating the position vector, we get [MATH: v|= (dr)/(dt); = ⟨(dx)/(dt), (dy)/(dt)⟩; = ⟨(d)/(dt)(t^{2} − 2t), (d)/(dt)(t^{3} − 3t)⟩; = ⟨2t − 2, 3t^{2} − 3⟩.]

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. This gives, [MATH: v(t)|= 0; ⟨2t − 2, 3t^{2} − 3⟩|= ⟨0, 0⟩.]

So we need [MATH: 2t − 2|= 0⇒t = 1,; 3t^{2} − 3|= 0⇒t = ± 1.]

Note that [MATH: t=-1] is outside of the domain of [MATH: t,] so we discard it.

The solution [MATH: t=1] is the only solution that satisfies both equations, so this is the only time when the object is stationary.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We can find the velocity [MATH: v(t)] of a moving particle moving up and down the [MATH: x]-axis by computing the derivative of its position function [MATH: x(t).] This same idea works in [MATH: 2] dimensions as well.

Content:
In two dimensions, we can represent a particle's position using a vector-valued function
[MATH: \mathbf{r} = \langle x(t), y(t)\rangle,]
which gives the particle's position relative to a fixed origin [MATH: O] at time [MATH: t.]

Content:
Here, [MATH: x(t)] tells us how the [MATH: x]-coordinate of the particle changes with time, and [MATH: y(t)] does the same for the [MATH: y]-coordinate. As time progresses, the particle moves along a path, and its position vector [MATH: \mathbf{r}(t)] changes with time.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/15fb899793084d902c8d4f698fad35ed]

Content:
The particle's velocity vector is then given by the derivative of its position vector,

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{v} = \frac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{r}}{\textrm{d}t}
= \left\langle \frac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t},\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t} \right\rangle.]

Content:
In other words, we differentiate the [MATH: x]-coordinate and the [MATH: y]-coordinate independently with respect to time. The resulting derivatives are the [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] components of the velocity vector.

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Velocity Vector of a Particle Moving in Two Dimensions

Example Prompt:
The position vector [MATH: \mathbf{r}] of a particle [MATH: P] relative to a fixed origin [MATH: O] at time [MATH: t > 0] is given by
[MATH: \mathbf{r} = \langle 3t^3, 2t^2\rangle.]
Calculate the velocity vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

[MATH: v|= (dr)/(dt); = ⟨(dx)/(dt), (dy)/(dt)⟩; = ⟨(d)/(dt)(3t^{3}), (d)/(dt)(2t^{2})⟩; = ⟨9t^{2}, 4t⟩.]

Item 8 — Tutorial: The Speed of a Particle

Content:
If the velocity of a particle at time [MATH: t] is

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{v} = \left< u, v \right> = \left< \dfrac{\textrm dx}{\textrm dt}, \, \dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dt} \right>,]

Content:
then its speed is given by the magnitude [MATH: |\mathbf{v}|,] as follows:
[MATH: |\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{ u^2 + v^2}	= \sqrt{\left(\frac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}]

---

Item 9 — Example: Calculating the Speed of a Particle at a Given Time

Calculate the speed of the particle at time [MATH: t=2.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we calculate the velocity vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}.] Differentiating the position vector, we get

[MATH: v|= (dr)/(dt); = ⟨(dx)/(dt), (dy)/(dt)⟩; = ⟨(d)/(dt)(6t^{2} + 2), (d)/(dt)(2t^{3})⟩; = ⟨12t, 6t^{2}⟩.]

To find the velocity when [MATH: t=2], we substitute into the above:
[MATH: v(2)|= ⟨12(2), 6(2)^{2}⟩; = ⟨24, 24⟩.]

To find the speed at [MATH: t=2] we calculate the magnitude of [MATH: \mathbf{v}(2),] and we get

[MATH: |v(2)||= sqrt(24^{2} + 24^{2}); = sqrt(2(24^{2})); = 24sqrt(2).]

So, the speed when [MATH: t=2] is [MATH: 24\sqrt{2}\approx 33.94] to two decimal places.
